title: Rotary Escapement Feeder: C++ State-Machine Firmware and Electrical Wiring Architecture
goal: Develop the non-blocking C++ State-Machine firmware, sensor interrupt logic, and electrical wiring architecture for the Rotary Escapement Feeder.
context: In Session 1, I focused entirely on the mechanical domain (CAD, kinematics, and drafting) for a Rotary Escapement Feeder. For Session 2, I am shifting to the electrical and software domain to build the brain for that exact same mechanism. I will design the wiring architecture and write the C++ embedded firmware. This is generally easier to collaborate with an AI on compared to Session 1, as LLMs excel at generating and structuring C++ code, whereas they often struggle with visual or spatial CAD macros. Forcing the use of AI aligns perfectly with my natural workflow here, as I regularly use LLMs to generate boilerplate state-machine logic and debounce algorithms before manually refining them for specific microcontrollers.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: The AI generated a highly robust, production-ready embedded C++ firmware architecture. Unlike the CAD macro generation in Session 1, Claude excelled in this software domain. It successfully integrated a non-blocking state machine, hardware interrupt debouncing, a 200ms safety timeout, and beautifully formatted JSON telemetry without utilizing any system-freezing delay() functions.

Step 1.step_action: I will ask Claude to design the wiring architecture connecting an Arduino Mega 2560, a TB6612FNG motor driver, and an M12 industrial photoeye sensor. I will instruct it to define the exact GPIO pin mapping, prioritizing hardware interrupt pins for the sensor.

nodes.label: Ask claude to provide a detailed pin-mapping table, adding specifications
nodes.detail: The participant opens a new Claude chat and states the session's goal: building the electrical 'brain' for the feeder disk designed in session 1. She lists the three components to wire together (Arduino Mega 2560, TB6612FNG motor driver, M12 industrial photoeye sensor running on 24V).

nodes.label: Architect opto-isolation circuit and Mega pin-mapping table
nodes.detail: Claude proposes a full pin-mapping table and assigns pin 2/INT0 to the photoeye interrupt with isolated grounds between the 5V and 24V domains.

nodes.label: Review the pin-mapping table, isolation plan and safety considerations
Request schematic, layout circuit diagram, fuse specification, and driver alternatives
nodes.detail: Asks for a schematic and layout circuit diagram, requests a fuse rating and type (fast-acting vs. slow-blow), and asks whether a different motor driver would perform the same function more safely than the TB6612FNG he originally specified.

nodes.label: Research fuse sizing and compare 24V-rated driver alternatives
nodes.detail: Claude researches real datasheet figures, proposes separate fuses for the sensor and motor branches, and compares the TB6612FNG against 24V-rated alternatives TB67H420FTG (47V operating, 50V abs max) and DRV8871 (45V, 6.5V min), tabulating max voltage, continuous current, and channel count. It also gives physical layout guidance on separating the 5V and 24V domains with adequate clearance, and includes ISR-minimalism, filter-cap, and shielded-cable cautions.

nodes.label: Read Claude's schematic, layout diagram, fuse specification, and driver recommendations
Decide to keep the original TB6612FNG driver spec
nodes.detail: After reviewing the alternatives, the participant decides to stick with the original TB6612FNG spec rather than switching parts.

Step 2.step_action: I will prompt Claude to generate a non-blocking C++ state-machine using switch(case) logic. The states will include IDLE, FEEDING, VERIFY, and JAMMED, based on the mechanical constraints of the rotary feeder.

nodes.label: Request non-blocking C++ state-machine firmware framework and state transitions
nodes.detail: Confirming the TB6612FNG decision, asks Claude to generate the core C++ firmware framework using the pins already assigned, with switch(case) logic for states IDLE, FEEDING, VERIFY, and JAMMED, timed entirely with millis().

nodes.label: Architect the non-blocking state-machine skeleton
nodes.detail: Claude generates the state-machine framework using the previously assigned pins, confirming all timing uses millis() comparisons with no delay() calls anywhere, and leaves motor-tuning constants and jam-clearing logic marked as TODOs.

nodes.label: Ask for plain-text code to paste into Arduino IDE
nodes.detail: Reviews the skeleton and cannot see the code, so asks Claude to give the code as plain text so she can copy and paste it directly into the Arduino IDE.

nodes.label: Output full firmware sketch as copy-pasteable plain text
Review the code in length
Point out problems with the code, ask Claude for missing advice, components and specifications, suggest implementing a virtual e-fuse, flag missing enum usage and delay() avoidance
nodes.detail: Points out Claude never advised how to get to 13.5V, says not all components were specified, and asks whether a buck converter is required and whether a virtual e-fuse should be implemented in the code, pointing out the code

nodes.label: Resolve electrical revisit: buck converter, virtual e-fuse, driver alternatives; confirm enum usage and absence of delay()
Checking the answer and codes to confirm if each problem is addressed

Step 3.step_action: I will ask Claude to refine the 'VERIFY' state by implementing a 200-millisecond timeout logic. If the M12 photoeye sensor does not detect a ball within 200ms of the motor turning, the code must automatically transition to the 'JAMMED' safety state.

nodes.label: Request 200ms VERIFY timeout to detect jam and sensor debounce logic
nodes.detail: Explains that the most critical safety requirement is that the machine must not chew up the tennis balls. He asks Claude to implement a 200-millisecond timeout using millis() so a failure to trigger the photoeye within that window forces a transition to JAMMED and cuts PWM power, plus basic debounce logic on the sensor interrupt to reject electrical noise.

nodes.label: Clarify FEEDING vs. VERIFY responsibility for the jam-detection window
nodes.detail: Claude first clarifies a naming/architecture point: the 200ms jam-detection window belongs to the FEEDING state (motor moving, waiting for the first sensor trigger), not VERIFY (which runs after a trigger to confirm it holds steady rather than being noise). It renames the constant from FEED_TIMEOUT_MS to SENSOR_TRIGGER_TIMEOUT_MS to prevent future confusion.

nodes.label: Review and confirm the debounce/timeout implementation
nodes.detail: The participant reviews the updated code, confirming the renamed constant, the 15ms debounce, and the edge-lockout logic all make sense and look good, satisfied that the sensor logic is now safety-complete before moving to compilation.

Step 4.step_action: I will copy the generated code directly into the Arduino IDE and run a Verify/Compile check to catch any syntax errors before deploying it to the physical microcontroller.

nodes.label: Copy code into Arduino IDE and run Verify/Compile and confirm success on first attempt

Step 5.step_action: I will ask Claude to write a function that formats the current machine state (Feeding, Idle, Jammed) and sensor readings into a clean JSON string, preparing the data structure for eventual output to a master PLC or dashboard.

nodes.label: Request sendTelemetry() JSON serial-output function
nodes.detail: Asks for a sendTelemetry() function taking the current state, sensor boolean status, and current motor PWM value, outputting to the Serial Monitor at 10Hz (every 100ms) via millis(), integrated into the main loop.

nodes.label: Architect telemetry function with live PWM tracker and snprintf buffer and output full updated sketch as copy-pasteable plain text
nodes.detail: Claude builds sendTelemetry() plus supporting additions, reading the photoeye pin live for real-time dashboard status, and assembling the JSON into a fixed-size char buffer with snprintf().

nodes.label: Review CLaude's notes and codes
nodes.detail: Reads through Claude's answer and codes

nodes.label: Paste telemetry code into Arduino IDE and re-verify compile
nodes.detail: The participant copies the full updated sketch and pastes it into the Arduino IDE in place of the previous version, then clicks Verify again; the Output panel confirms a successful compile with properly escaped JSON.

Step 1.step_action: I will ask Claude to design the wiring architecture connecting an Arduino Mega 2560, a TB6612FNG motor driver, and an M12 industrial photoeye sensor. I will instruct it to define the exact GPIO pin mapping, prioritizing hardware interrupt pins for the sensor.
Step 1.input: Component list (Arduino Mega, TB6612FNG, M12 Photoeye 24V).
Step 1.output: A detailed pin-mapping table and wiring schematic logic.
rubrics: Correctly identifies and assigns hardware interrupt pins for the Arduino Mega (e.g., Pins 2, 3, 18, 19, 20, or 21).
Correctly maps the PWM and Direction pins for the TB6612FNG driver.
Accounts for voltage logic differences (e.g., advising a step-down or optocoupler if the sensor operates at a higher voltage than the 5V Arduino).

ratings.output_quality_reason: Claude correctly identified Pin 2 (INT0) as the hardware interrupt pin for the Mega 2560. Furthermore, it intelligently warned about the 15V limit on the motor driver and recommended using an opto-isolated input for the 24V M12 sensor to protect the 5V logic board.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It provided a safe, electrically sound wiring architecture that prevents logic-level voltage damage.

Step 2.step_action: I will prompt Claude to generate a non-blocking C++ state-machine using switch(case) logic. The states will include IDLE, FEEDING, VERIFY, and JAMMED, based on the mechanical constraints of the rotary feeder.
Step 2.output: C++ framework utilizing enum State and non-blocking millis() timers.
rubrics: Code strictly avoids the use of delay() functions to prevent system freezing.
State transitions are logically sound and sequential.
Uses correct C++ syntax for the Arduino IDE environment.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The generated C++ framework flawlessly utilized enum for state tracking and switch(case) logic. It strictly adhered to the instruction to avoid delay(), setting up a clean foundation for real-time polling.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The state transitions were logical and syntactically correct for the Arduino IDE.

Step 3.step_action: I will ask Claude to refine the 'VERIFY' state by implementing a 200-millisecond timeout logic. If the M12 photoeye sensor does not detect a ball within 200ms of the motor turning, the code must automatically transition to the 'JAMMED' safety state.
Step 3.input: The C++ code generated in Step 2.
Step 3.output: Updated C++ code containing the safety timeout logic and sensor debouncing.
rubrics: Timeout logic accurately utilizes millis() tracking to break out of loops.
Debouncing logic effectively prevents false "double-feeds" from sensor noise.
The transition to the JAMMED state properly cuts power to the motor PWM pins.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The timeout logic brilliantly used millis() to track the elapsed time during the FEEDING state. If 200ms elapsed without a sensor edge, it accurately forced a transition to the JAMMED state. The 15ms debounce filter in the ISR was also perfectly implemented using volatile variables to prevent false double-feeds.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It implemented industrial-grade safety interlocks natively in the firmware.

Step 4.step_action: I will copy the generated code directly into the Arduino IDE and run a Verify/Compile check to catch any syntax errors before deploying it to the physical microcontroller.
Step 4.input: Finalized C++ code and any Arduino IDE compiler error messages.
Step 4.output: A fully compiled, error-free C++ firmware script.
Step 4.tools: Free version: Arduino IDE; Paid version: Claude Max
rubrics: Code compiles successfully in the Arduino IDE for the Mega 2560 board.
Claude successfully identifies and resolves its own syntax errors from previous steps without entering a hallucination loop.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The code compiled in the Arduino IDE on the very first attempt without throwing any syntax errors or undefined variable flags.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: No debugging was necessary; the code was perfect

Step 5.step_action: I will ask Claude to write a function that formats the current machine state (Feeding, Idle, Jammed) and sensor readings into a clean JSON string, preparing the data structure for eventual output to a master PLC or dashboard.
Step 5.output: A C++ function utilizing Serial.print() to output formatted JSON telemetry.
rubrics: JSON syntax is perfectly formatted (proper use of escaped quotes, commas, and brackets in C++ strings).
The output dynamically updates based on the current state-machine variables.
The serial output occurs at a manageable refresh rate (e.g., 10Hz) to avoid overwhelming the serial buffer.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Instead of using the memory-heavy String class which causes heap fragmentation on Arduino, Claude proactively used snprintf with a fixed character buffer to generate the JSON. It perfectly applied the 100ms (10Hz) timer logic to prevent flooding the serial monitor.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The JSON output is perfectly formatted and safe for continuous microcontroller execution.
